findings.lesson_text: Iago commands her to be silent: "Charlot, I charge thee hold thy peace."
findings.issue: The word 'Charlot' does not exist in the play. The quoted line 'Charlot, I charge thee hold thy peace' is not from Othello. Iago's actual line when silencing Emilia in Act 5 Scene 2 is 'Go to! Charm your tongue.' (Folger edition, line 3465). The lesson has fabricated a Shakespeare quotation, presenting a made-up line as a real quotation students will use in exam essays.
findings.canonical_truth: Iago's command to Emilia in Act 5 Scene 2 is: 'With Cassio, mistress. Go to! Charm your tongue.' (Folger line 3465). There is no word 'Charlot' in the scene; Iago uses other terms of abuse ('villainous whore', 'filth') elsewhere in the scene but not at this specific moment of silencing Emilia.

findings.lesson_text: When Othello reveals that Iago told him of the affair, Emilia is horrified: "My husband!" (repeated three times, each with escalating disbelief).
findings.issue: Emilia says 'My husband!' (or 'My husband?') four times in rapid succession, not three. The Folger edition records the exclamation at lines 3417, 3418, 3424, and 3428 — four separate utterances. Othello himself remarks 'What needs this iteration, woman?' after the third, and a fourth follows. Students told it is three times will give incorrect detail in close-analysis answers.
findings.canonical_truth: In Act 5 Scene 2, Emilia says 'My husband?' four times (Folger lines 3417, 3418, 3424, 3428) as Othello identifies Iago as the source of the false accusations. Othello's line 'What needs this iteration, woman?' comes after the third utterance, with a fourth following shortly after.

findings.lesson_text: Act 3, Scene 3 is the play's pivotal scene — the longest in Shakespeare's canon.
findings.issue: Act 3 Scene 3 of Othello is not the longest scene in Shakespeare's canon. According to Wikipedia's List of Shakespearean Scenes, The Winter's Tale Act 4 Scene 4 runs to approximately 895 lines — substantially longer than Othello 3.3 which is approximately 531 lines. Other scenes (King John 2.1 at ~609 lines, Hamlet 2.2 at ~600 lines) also exceed it. The claim will mislead students who cite it as a factual statistic in exam essays.
findings.canonical_truth: Othello Act 3 Scene 3 is the longest scene in Othello and one of the longest in Shakespeare's tragedies (~531 lines). However, it is not the longest scene in the Shakespeare canon; that distinction belongs to The Winter's Tale Act 4 Scene 4 (~895 lines). The lesson should describe 3.3 as Othello's longest scene rather than the longest in the entire canon.

findings.lesson_text: At the end of Act 1, Iago reveals his plan in soliloquy. He will use Cassio's good looks and charm ("A fellow almost damned in a fair wife") to make Othello believe Desdemona is unfaithful.
findings.issue: The line 'A fellow almost damned in a fair wife' does not appear in Iago's end-of-Act-1 soliloquy (Act 1 Scene 3). It appears in Act 1 Scene 1 (lines 22-23), where Iago complains to Roderigo that Othello promoted Cassio over him. Furthermore, the lesson's gloss — 'Cassio's good looks and charm' — misreads the line: 'almost damned in a fair wife' means Cassio is compromised or near-ruined by having an attractive wife, not that he himself is charming. Iago's actual end-of-Act-1 soliloquy describes Cassio as 'a proper man' with 'a smooth dispose / To be suspected, framed to make women false' (Act 1 Sc 3, Folger lines 0769-0770), which is where the idea of Cassio's attractiveness belongs — but that is distinct from the misattributed quote.
findings.canonical_truth: 'A fellow almost damned in a fair wife' is Iago's description of Cassio in Act 1 Scene 1 (lines 22-23), spoken to Roderigo as he explains why Cassio got the lieutenancy. The phrase refers to Cassio being (in Iago's contemptuous view) nearly damned because of or through his association with a beautiful woman — not a compliment about Cassio's personal attractiveness. The end-of-Act-1-Sc-3 soliloquy ('Thus do I ever make my fool my purse') does describe Cassio as 'a proper man' but does not contain the 'almost damned' quote.

findings.lesson_text: Shakespeare creates sustained dramatic irony through the word 'honest.' Iago is called 'honest Iago' over fifty times in the play.
findings.issue: The word 'honest' (and related forms) appears approximately 40-45 times in Othello, not over fifty. The Folger Library's own language notes and SparkNotes' style analysis describe the word appearing 'more than forty times.' Stating 'over fifty' is an overcount that students may cite as a specific factual statistic in their exam essays.
findings.canonical_truth: The word 'honest' appears approximately 40-45 times in Othello across all characters (Folger; SparkNotes style notes: 'more than forty times'). The lesson should say 'more than forty times' rather than 'over fifty times.'
